title: Presidential Elections, 1796 and 1800
snippet: How each state's electors voted in 1796 and 1800, with Marbury v. Madison and McCulloch v. Maryland.
description:
Question: How did the first political parties divide the country?

Ideas for one lesson in MapMaker (choose any):

  • Compare the elections of 1796 and 1800. Each pie shows how a state's electors voted for John Adams (Federalist) and Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican); bigger pies mean more electors. Which regions backed each party, and which states split?
  • Click Marbury v. Madison (1803) and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) for the question, the ruling and why each matters.
  • Sketch pins for the First Bank of the United States (Philadelphia, 1791) and Washington's Farewell Address (published in Philadelphia, 1796).
  • Download an image or export a PDF of the map to keep the work.

Notes: In 1796 and 1800 each elector cast two votes for president, so a state's votes add up to twice its electors. The pies show only the votes for Adams and Jefferson; each pop-up lists every candidate. In 1800, Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied with 73 votes each, so the House of Representatives chose the president: Jefferson, on 17 February 1801. The 12th Amendment (1804) then gave electors separate votes for president and vice president. The National Archives' 1800 table shows a dash for Virginia's Aaron Burr, but its own Burr total of 73 needs Virginia's 21. Today's state outlines (Natural Earth, public domain), with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia. Territories aren't shown.

Sources: National Archives (electoral votes and court cases); Natural Earth (outlines).

Version 1.2 (14 October 2026).
